metadata.title: Does increasing hours of schooling lead to improvements in student learning?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This policy brief uses PIRLS 2006 and PIRLS 2011 contextual and achievement information aggregated at the country/benchmarking-participant level (e.g., average classroom hours and average reading achievement). The analysis described is based on cross-cycle comparisons and country-level correlations/changes rather than student-level model estimation, so the brief does not specify the application of PIRLS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the document does not report any weight variable names (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or variance estimation approach, weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text. For analysts working with PIRLS microdata, the appropriate approach would be to apply PIRLS complex survey weights when estimating student-level relationships and to use the IEA-provided replicate weights for standard errors; however, this brief’s reported results are presented as descriptive/correlation-based country summaries.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The brief reports country-level averages and correlations between time-in-school indicators and average reading achievement, rather than fitting a PV-based student-level achievement model. As a result, plausible-value handling is not applicable to the way the outcomes are presented in this policy brief. Missing-data handling is not described because the brief does not provide the underlying microdata processing steps (e.g., exclusions/imputation rules) needed to assess how missing questionnaire or achievement inputs were handled.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2006 and PIRLS 2011 data for the set of countries/benchmarking participants that participated in both cycles (Table 1 lists the overlapping systems). The brief estimates total annual classroom hours from principals’ reports in the PIRLS school questionnaire (school days per year and instructional hours per day) and derives effective teaching time from teacher-reported proportions of time devoted to whole-class/small-group instruction (PIRLS 2006 only, since this information was not available in PIRLS 2011). For the effective teaching time analysis, the brief reports results for the subset of 12 of the 36 education systems with available effective teaching time information.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA policy brief uses PIRLS 2006 and PIRLS 2011 to examine whether increasing students’ time in school is associated with reading achievement at the fourth-grade level. It constructs two time indicators: (1) total annual classroom hours estimated from principals’ reports (school days per year and instructional hours per day) and (2) effective teaching time defined as the proportion of classroom time devoted to teaching-related tasks, excluding administrative and disciplinary activities (available from PIRLS 2006 teacher reports). Across 36 overlapping education systems, most countries increased classroom hours between 2006 and 2011, but changes in hours were not consistently associated with changes in average reading achievement. Correlations between classroom hours and reading achievement in PIRLS 2011 were small and non-significant across systems. In contrast, effective teaching time showed a more favorable association: in 12 systems with available data, the relationship was significantly positive in several countries, suggesting that how instructional time is used may matter more than simply increasing total hours. The brief does not report student-level modeling details, plausible-value handling, or missing-data procedures, limiting causal interpretation.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a policy brief summarizing descriptive and correlation-based analyses using PIRLS cycle-level and country-level aggregates rather than an empirical ML study with a reported predictive modeling pipeline. As such, there are no ML algorithms, no PV-based student-level outcome modeling, and no reported sample sizes at the student level in the provided text. The extraction therefore leaves total_students and per-country n_students as null because the brief presents results in terms of country averages and correlations without microdata sample tables.
